content: Ammonium bicarbonate, also known as bicarbonate of ammonia, ammonium hydrogen carbonate, hartshorn, or powdered baking ammonia, is the bicarbonate salt of ammonia. It is synthesized by passing carbon dioxide through a solution of ammonia, resulting in the deposition of a white, odorless powder that is only slightly soluble in water. When exposed to air or heated, an aqueous solution of ammonium bicarbonate releases carbon dioxide and becomes alkaline. Upon boiling, aqueous solutions of all carbonates, including ammonium bicarbonate, decompose, releasing carbon dioxide and the substance that reacted with the carbonate ion to form the bicarbonate—in this case, ammonia. At room temperature, ammonium bicarbonate appears as a white crystalline powder with a faint ammonia odor. It dissolves in water to form a mildly alkaline solution but is insoluble in acetone and alcohols. When heated to temperatures between 36°C and 60°C, it decomposes into ammonia, carbon dioxide, and water vapor in an endothermic reaction, which causes a cooling effect. Reactions with acids produce carbon dioxide, while reactions with alkalis release ammonia. Historically, ammonium bicarbonate was used as a leavening agent in baking (e.g., for gingerbread or Chinese youtiao) before the introduction of baking soda. It is still used in some food products alongside baking soda. Scandinavian cookbooks may refer to it as hartshorn or horn salt, and it can be substituted with baking soda. In China, ammonium bicarbonate has been widely used as an inexpensive nitrogen fertilizer, but it is being replaced by urea due to its lower quality and instability. Beyond agriculture, it is utilized in the production of fire-extinguishing compounds, pharmaceuticals, dyes, pigments, and as a source of ammonia in basic fertilizers. It also finds applications in the plastic and rubber industries, ceramics manufacturing, chrome leather tanning, and the synthesis of catalysts. Ammonium bicarbonate is an irritant to the skin, eyes, and respiratory system. Additionally, acrylamide, a compound formed during the baking process when using ammonium bicarbonate, has been linked to cancer in laboratory animals.
